doc.title: Dave Rivello interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rochester, New York, January 11, 2012

title: Designing the twelve-piece ensemble
summary: He chose twelve pieces in 1993, influenced by Gil Evans: soprano, tenor, bass clarinet, tuba, flugelhorn, no alto or baritone.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played what: early band size and instrumentation

blocks.x: If you could have a seventeen piece big band, would you? Or do you like the twelve?

No actually I like the twelve. To me it’s the perfect number. And the reason that I came up with that sized band, in 1993, was I had written a lot of music for standard jazz ensembles. And I realized that by then, and having gone through Eastman and everything with my degree, that I could do four note trombone voicings in my sleep. And so I thought wow I’m kind of stuck here. So what can I do? Well if I take some instruments away, then I have to figure out how to do this. And so I’ve created my own good problem to move myself forward. Also I’ve been, besides Brookmeyer, very influenced, and I mean Gil Evans is just a master at everything. So I kind of looked at Gil Evans’ bands and they were never full-sized bands. And so I thought wow, so what would be my dream ensemble? And so I decided that I like alto saxophone, but I really like soprano saxophone. So my band has no alto.

Soprano, and he doubles on flute. And then tenor sax of course, and he doubles on flute and clarinet. And I like baritone saxophone but I really like bass clarinet. So there’s no baritone saxophone in my band, it’s bass clarinet and he doubles on flute and clarinet. And then, because of Gil Evans’ influence probably, I wanted to have a tuba. So two

trombones and a tuba. And then I thought about having French horn, also from Gil’s influence, but I thought if I’ve got one non-jazz guy, a tuba player, and I’m in Rochester, New York, two is probably going to be too much of a gamble. So I decided I have two trumpet players and I have the third guy only plays flugelhorn. So I think of that as kind of a French horn that blows forward instead of backwards. And that was I don’t have to deal with the acoustical issues of that also. And then piano, bass and drums, the standard jazz rhythm section. And so that’s my dream ensemble. And no matter what situation there would be, if I could I would just write for my own band all the time.
You’ve already got a built-in start on your own sound too with that instrumentation.

Right. And what I knew when I did it too, thinking ahead, is that it would be problematic in that college bands that are seventeen or sixteen piece bands, that it doesn’t work so well for them because what are they going to do with the other people, they’ll be running around the halls throwing erasers and causing trouble. But for me, that’s my dream band to write for. My goal was to just continue writing for that band as I can in and around freelance work, and just create a book, a body of work that is my work for that ensemble.
